\chapter{Data Description}
\label{chap:data}

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
This chapter describes the two public datasets used in this thesis.
SKM-TEA~\cite{desai2021skmtea} provides the knee \gls{mri} volumes from which the six continual-learning tasks are built, and AeroPath~\cite{støverud2023aeropathairwaysegmentationbenchmark} provides the chest \gls{ct} volumes of the control task.
\Cref{tab:ch4_datasets} summarises both datasets.
The chapter then describes how the volumes are split, how the few-shot training subsets are drawn, how the data are preprocessed, and which properties of the data limit the conclusions that can be drawn from them.

\section{SKM-TEA}
\label{sec:data-skmtea}

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
The Stanford Knee MRI with Multi-Task Evaluation (SKM-TEA) dataset contains knee \gls{mri} scans of 155 patients acquired at Stanford Healthcare~\cite{desai2021skmtea}.
We chose SKM-TEA because VoxTell performs poorly on it (\cref{sec:intro-motivation}).
SKM-TEA is distributed under the terms of the Stanford University School of Medicine and of the Lower Extremity Radiographs dataset~\cite[App.~A.5]{desai2021skmtea}.
We signed the Stanford AIMI research-use agreement before downloading the data.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
All scans were acquired with the 3D \gls{qdess} sequence on one of two 3\,T GE MR750 scanners, with patient consent and approval of the Stanford University Institutional Review Board~\cite{desai2021skmtea}.
\gls{qdess} acquires two inherently registered 3D echoes with different contrasts.
SKM-TEA is distributed in two benchmark tracks, one based on raw k-space data and one based on the scanner-generated \gls{dicom} images.
We use the \gls{dicom} track, which stores the images and segmentations of each scan in one \gls{hdf5} file~\cite{skmtea_dataset_doc}.
We use only the first of the two echoes, as the dataset authors do in the segmentation part of their tutorial~\cite{skmtea_tutorial}.
The dataset also provides versioned annotation files that list the scans of each split defined by the dataset authors, with metadata such as the voxel size~\cite{skmtea_dataset_doc}.
All 155 volumes have a voxel size of $0.3125 \times 0.3125 \times 0.8$\,mm.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
Six tissues were segmented manually on all \gls{dicom} images: patellar cartilage, femoral cartilage, medial and lateral tibial cartilage, and medial and lateral meniscus~\cite{desai2021skmtea}.
The segmentations were drawn slice by slice in the sagittal plane and then corrected for volumetric consistency in the axial and coronal planes~\cite[App.~A.4]{desai2021skmtea}.
Each scan was labelled by one of two researchers with three to four years of experience in knee \gls{mri} interpretation, supervised by two board-certified musculoskeletal radiologists.
The dataset therefore contains no information on the agreement between annotators.
The dataset also provides bounding boxes for sixteen pathology categories, which we do not use.
According to the annotation files, 130 of the 155 scans contain at least one of these pathologies.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
Each of the six segmented structures defines one task.
The text prompt of a task is the name of its structure in lower case: ``patellar cartilage'', ``femoral cartilage'', ``medial tibial cartilage'', ``lateral tibial cartilage'', ``medial meniscus'' and ``lateral meniscus''.
% source: prompt column of results/data_stats/skm_tea_volumes.csv
The same text prompt is used for training and evaluation, and its wording is not varied.
Of the six structures, the four cartilages are among VoxTell's training labels, whereas the two menisci are not~\cite[Suppl.~Table~10]{rokuss2025voxtellfreetextpromptableuniversal}.
Since all six structures are labelled in every volume, the six tasks share the same 155 volumes and differ only in the target structure.
The structures are small, with median volumes from 1.90\,cm$^3$ (lateral meniscus) to 10.99\,cm$^3$ (femoral cartilage), and lie next to each other in the knee joint (\cref{fig:ch4_examples}).
% source: stdout of scripts/plot_data.py (structure voxel counts x voxel size of the official annotation files, all 155 volumes)
The order in which the tasks are trained is part of the experimental setup and is given in \cref{subsec:exp-data}.

\section{AeroPath}
\label{sec:data-aeropath}

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
AeroPath contains 27 contrast-enhanced chest \gls{ct} scans (\gls{cta}) of patients undergoing diagnostic tests for lung cancer, acquired with a thorax lung protocol at St.\ Olavs Hospital in Trondheim, Norway~\cite{støverud2023aeropathairwaysegmentationbenchmark}.
Data collection was approved by the regional ethics committee, and the patients gave written informed consent.
The dataset is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence~\cite{aeropath_zenodo}.
AeroPath provides the control task, for which we use only the lung label of each volume, with the text prompt ``lung''.
Neither the publication nor the dataset repository or the Zenodo record documents how the lung labels were created, so it is unknown whether they are manual or automatic references.
% source: github.com/MIC-DKFZ/VoxTell/issues/15 (maintainer comment 2026-10-02: 'Datasets added in v1.1' lists AeroPath), checked 2026-11-07
AeroPath was a held-out test set in the VoxTell paper~\cite[Suppl.~Table~7]{rokuss2025voxtellfreetextpromptableuniversal}, but it is among the sources added to the training data of checkpoint v1.1, which we use~\cite{rokuss2026voxtellissue15}; ``lung'' is a VoxTell training label in 3{,}427 training cases~\cite[Suppl.~Table~10]{rokuss2025voxtellfreetextpromptableuniversal}.

\section{Data Splits and Few-Shot Subsets}
\label{sec:data-splits}

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
We split each dataset once, at random.
After shuffling the volumes with a fixed random seed (42), we assign the first 70\,\% of the shuffled list to the training split, the next 15\,\% to the validation split and the remaining volumes to the test split.
This gives 108 training, 23 validation and 24 test volumes for SKM-TEA and 19, 4 and 4 volumes for AeroPath.
Of the AeroPath volumes, we use only the 4 test volumes, to evaluate the control task.
Because the six tasks share the same volumes, all tasks and all experiments in this thesis use the same split.
Each SKM-TEA patient contributes exactly one scan, so no patient appears in more than one split.
The validation volumes are used to monitor training and, in an additional evaluation, to select the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss (\cref{sec:method-adaptation}).
All reported results are computed on the test volumes.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
SKM-TEA also defines an official split of 86 training, 33 validation and 36 test scans, whose test set consists of the 36 patients who received additional arthroscopic surgery~\cite{desai2021skmtea}.
We use our own random split instead, which, unlike the official split, does not allow a comparison with published SKM-TEA results.
For comparing continual-learning strategies with each other, it is sufficient that all strategies use the same split.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
For the few-shot experiments, we reduce the training split to its first $k$ volumes in the order of the shuffled list, where $k \in \{5, 10, 20\}$ is the number of labelled training volumes per task.
The subsets are therefore nested, with the 5 volumes contained in the 10 and the 10 contained in the 20.
For each $k$, all six tasks use the same $k$ volumes.
Only one subset is drawn for each $k$, so we cannot measure how much the results depend on which volumes are chosen.
Runs with the full training split use all 108 training volumes.
The validation and test volumes are the same for every $k$ and for the full training split.

\section{Preprocessing}
\label{sec:data-preprocessing}

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
We convert each SKM-TEA \gls{hdf5} file into two \gls{nifti} files, one for the first echo and one for the labels.
In the \gls{hdf5} file, the segmentation is stored as six binary channels, one per tissue.
We merge them into a single label map, in which unlabelled voxels take the value 0 and labelled voxels the number of their channel in the order of the dataset documentation~\cite{skmtea_dataset_doc}: 1 for patellar cartilage, 2 for femoral cartilage, 3 for medial tibial cartilage, 4 for lateral tibial cartilage, 5 for medial meniscus and 6 for lateral meniscus.
The binary target mask of a task consists of the voxels with that task's label value.
The \gls{nifti} files are written with an identity affine, so they store neither the voxel size nor the orientation of the scan.
Images and labels come from the same voxel grid, so they stay aligned.
The AeroPath volumes and labels are used in their original \gls{nifti} format.

% CLAUDE-DRAFT
When a volume is loaded, it is reoriented according to its affine and cropped to the bounding box of its non-zero voxels.
The reorientation leaves the SKM-TEA volumes unchanged because their affine is the identity.
According to the annotation files, 18 of the 155 SKM-TEA scans store the left--right axis in the opposite direction to the other 137.
% source: field 'orientation' of results/data_stats/skm_tea_annotations/v1.0.0/*.json: (SI, AP, LR) 137, (SI, AP, RL) 18
The intensities of each volume are then normalised to zero mean and unit standard deviation over the cropped volume, with the z-score normalisation of nnU-Net~\cite{isensee2018nnunetselfadaptingframeworkunetbased}.
The same normalisation is applied to the \gls{mri} and the \gls{ct} volumes.
The volumes are not resampled, so the network receives each volume on its stored voxel grid, and the voxel size in the affine has no effect on the input.
This preprocessing follows the configuration distributed with the VoxTell checkpoint, which uses z-score normalisation for all inputs, including \gls{ct}, and a preprocessing plan without resampling.\footnote{File \texttt{plans.json} of the checkpoint \texttt{voxtell\_v1.1} in the Hugging Face repository \texttt{mrokuss/VoxTell}: normalisation scheme \texttt{ZScoreNormalization}, no target spacing, image reader \texttt{NibabelIOWithReorient}.}
% source: code/models/voxtell_v1.1/plans.json (downloaded by code/scripts/download_checkpoint.py from mrokuss/VoxTell); code/src/data/preprocess.py
\Cref{sec:method-adaptation} describes how patches are sampled during training and how predictions are assembled during evaluation.
